    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):

        ]
    
        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))

        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats['output_range']
        ref_output_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_output_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e

They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n533\t\n534\t**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n535\t- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n536\t\n537\t**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n538\t1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\n539\t2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\n540\t3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\n541\t4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \n542\t5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \n543\t\n544\t**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n545\t1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n546\t2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\n547\t3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\n548\t4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\n549\t\n550\t**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \n551\t\n552\t**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \"Step 12\".\n553\t\n554\t---\n555\t\n556\t### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\n557\t\n558\t**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\n559\t\n560\t**Actions**:\n561\t- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\n562\t  - Key decisions and rationale\n563\t  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\n564\t  - Validation results and tables\n565\t  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\n566\t- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\n567\t  - Dataset description\n568\t  - How to load and use the converted data\n569\t  - Output format specification\n570\t  - Key statistics\n571\t- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\n572\t- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\n573\t\n574\t**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\n575\t\n576\t---\n577\t\n578\t## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\n579\t\n580\t**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Include both the \"Go\" and \"Catch\" trials, but exclude the \"Aborted\" and \"Auto-rewarded\" trials.\n\n### Decoder Inputs:\n\nNo inputs for this task.\n\n### Decoder Outputs\n\n- Image identity (of the image presented during the non-grey screen), categorical variable. Time-varying.\n- Image change, binary variable. Have value of 1 right after a change in image identity, otherwise 0. Time-varying.\n- Running speed, discretized into five equal percentile bins. Time-varying.\n- Pupil diameter, discretized into five equal percentile bins.  Time-varying.\n- Trial outcome. Static per-trial.\n\n## Target Data Format\n\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\n\n```python\ndata = {\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # list of sessions\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\n\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'metadata': {\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\n### Key Format Requirements\n\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\n\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \n\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\n\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\n\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \n\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\n\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. What variables in the raw data is `output` *Image change* derived from?\n\ni. Image change is a binary time-varying variable derived from `change_time` and the `go` column in the trials table. It is 1 only during the first image flash and following grey period (750ms window starting at `change_time`), and only for **go trials** where an actual image change occurs. For catch trials (sham change), `image_change` is 0 throughout.\n\nii.\n```python\nimage_change = np.zeros(n_frames, dtype=np.int8)\nif row['go']:\n    change_end_idx = np.searchsorted(ophys_ts[idx], row['change_time'] + 0.75)\n    image_change[change_idx:change_end_idx] = 1\n```\n\niii. The 750ms window corresponds to one stimulus flash (250ms) plus the following grey inter-stimulus interval (500ms). This marks only the transient change event rather than the entire post-change period. Catch trials are excluded because no actual image change occurs — the `go` column distinguishes real changes from sham changes.\n\n## 4-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Image change*?\n\ni. No processing beyond computing the binary indicator from `change_time` and `go` via `np.searchsorted`.\n\nii. See 3-a.\n\niii. Percentile-based binning ensures roughly equal class counts across bins, which is important for balanced decoding. Experiments with a non-zero probability of interictal events were then checked manually in order to exclude any potentially epileptic mice (see Steinmetz et al., 2017).\n90:Notice that this is taking a linear combination of the two (generally, adjacent) columns of the original image, using the decimal parts of the g function as coefficients. In the event that both f[j] and g[j - 1] are not nonnegative, then we fill that column with the average from the original image. And if f is nonnegative but g is not, then we simply replace that column with the exact same column from the original image.\n97:Suite2P's parameter maxregshift has a default value of 0.1, which clips lateral motions of more than 10% of the FOV dimension. We found a few examples in our release data where our experiments had real, long-timescale lateral shifts of greater than 10%. We increased the maxregshift parameter to 0.2, to allow for registration of these experiments. A consequence of this change was that up to 20% lateral shifts were allowed by Suite2P over short timescales as well. We observed that these short timescale shifts, often single frames, were likely not physical shifts, but struggles of the registration algorithm to register low signal-to-noise frames. Across an entire experiment, we monitor the worst-case shifts and establish a motion border which invalidates any ROI which touches it. To prevent too much inflation of the motion border exclusion area by these unphysical short timescale shifts, we detrended the x and y lateral corrections with a median filter over a 3 second window. We clip frame displacements to a +/-5% window around any outlier more than 5% above or below the detrended corrections was truncated to 5%. This allowed us to handle physical long timescale drifts and limit the impact of artifactual short timescale shifts. Any movie frames where the lateral shift was truncated were translated to the new truncated translation value.\n134:We return normalized, detrended traces of neuronal activity by performing the following algorithm on each trace. First, we estimate the standard deviation of the noise in the trace. We do this by centering the trace on the curve resulting from applying a median filter with kernel size 3.33 seconds to the trace. To avoid including signal events in our estimate of noise, we discard any values that exceed 1.5 times the absolute value of the minimum of this centered trace. We make a first estimate of the standard deviation of noise in the trace as 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of this truncated, centered trace. We further discard any values that exceed 2.5 times this first estimate of the standard deviation and finally return 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the remaining centered trace values as the standard deviation of noise in the trace.\n138:Finally, we detrend the dF/F trace. We estimate the trend in the dF/F trace by applying a median filter with kernel length 3.33 seconds. To prevent anomalously large trends from arising, we use the same algorithm we used to estimate the standard deviation of noise in the raw trace to estimate the standard deviation of noise in the dF/F trace. We constrain the trend to never exceed 2.5 times this estimated standard deviation of noise in the dF/F trace. A natural image appears for 250 ms followed by 500 ms gray; one image repeats until an identity change. Premature licking resets/delays the change and creates an aborted attempt.\n126\t- Go trials contain a real identity change; catch trials contain a sham change. Combined with behavior, requested outcomes are hit, miss, false alarm, and correct reject. Auto-rewarded and aborted trials are not valid choice trials.\n127\t- Behavioral analysis assigns events to each 750 ms image-presentation interval. Omitted flashes use the corresponding 750 ms interval.\n128\t- Reference neural analyses use inferred discrete calcium event magnitudes, not newly computed dF/F. Event extraction removes slow GCaMP decay dynamics. The whitepaper notes sampling-rate-aware noise estimation and compares 31 Hz to downsampled traces.\n129\t- For image response analyses, the paper uses 50-800 ms to account for neural latency. Its decoder uses the first 400 ms, concatenating each neuron's event samples per image.\n130\t- Running is open-loop and does not control task progression.\n131\t- Eye tracking fits pupil/eye/corneal-reflection ellipses. Processed `pupil_area` treats the observed ellipse major axis as the diameter of an underlying circular pupil. Frames marked likely blink (fit missing or area z-score >3, expanded by two adjacent frames) are represented as NaN.\n132\t- Single-plane and multiplane data have different native frame rates, so no fixed sample count can represent the same physical interval without temporal resampling/binning.\n133\t\n134\t### Curation Steps\n135\t\n136\t**Neuron curation rules**:\n137\t- Experiments undergo Allen Institute session QC. ROIs that are unions, duplicates/ghosts, non-cell objects, or otherwise invalid are excluded. AllenSDK `cell_specimen_table` already exposes only valid ROIs.\n138\t- The paper's focused biological analyses use selected familiar-image, multiplane sessions, but the decoder task requests the supplied Visual Behavior recordings generally; the implications are resolved in Steps 4-5.\n139\t\n140\t**Trial curation rules**:\n141\t- Include go and catch only; exclude aborted trials (lick before change) and auto-rewarded trials.\n142\t- Valid outcome classes are hit, miss, false alarm, and correct reject.\n143\t- Reference SDK performance metrics also exclude aborted trials.\n144\t\n145\t### Decoders Trained\n146\t| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n147\t|------------------|----------|\n148\t| Image change vs immediately preceding repeat | Cross-validated % correct shown graphically in Figure 6A; no exact numeric table in text. |\n149\t| Hit vs miss on image changes | Cross-validated % correct shown graphically in Figure 6C; no exact numeric table in text. |\n150\t\n151\tThe paper used 5-fold cross-validated random forests and reports means/SEM over imaging planes. repeat experiment's area index for every cell | experiment metadata | Each supplied experiment is one imaging plane in one area. |\n192\t\n193\t### Key Decisions\n194\t1. **Use active sessions only**: Exclude session types containing `passive`, because replayed passive changes receive artificial no-response outcomes and the paper excludes passive data.\n195\t2. **Use one imaging plane per decoder session**: Matches paper decoding and preserves homogeneous neuron populations; multiscope planes legitimately share behavioral labels.\n196\t3. **Use SDK filtered events**: Matches the paper's detected-event neural representation and uses SDK sampling-rate-aware filtering rather than recomputing dF/F.\n197\t4. **Retain SDK go/catch trial boundaries**: Keep only `go | catch`, which inherently excludes aborted and auto-rewarded rows. Trial matrices may have variable timepoint counts, while all use the same 100 ms bins.\n198\t5. **100 ms bins**: This common physical bin has roughly 1 sample for multiscope and 3 for single-plane data, provides enough temporal resolution for 250 ms images and the one-bin change pulse, and greatly limits memory. Event values are summed (not averaged) so each bin represents detected event magnitude in that duration.\n199\t6. **No alignment-event cropping**: Trials are segmented at native `start_time` and `stop_time`; the required segmentation is trial-based, not a fixed event-centered analysis. Metadata alignment is trial start (`off_start=0`, variable `off_end=None`).\n200\t7. **Image gray class**: The required identity is the image presented during non-gray screen. Gray periods and omitted flashes are class 0. Sixteen image names across sets A/B are globally stable classes.\n201\t8. **Behavior quintiles are fitted per experiment**: This yields equal percentile bins within each recording and avoids cross-rig calibration/units differences. Repeated quantile edges are handled monotonically; digitized labels are clipped to 0-4.\n202\t9. **Pupil diameter and missing values**: Use whitepaper-defined processed pupil area. Interpolate only over SDK-valid points; do not use raw blink-contaminated values. Exclude the three active experiments with no eye samples (795953296, 833631914, 806456687), because an entire required output cannot be imputed responsibly.\n203\t10. **Trace edges**: Use bins fully anchored to trial start, with `ceil((stop-start)/0.1)` centers and clip final edge to stop. Nearest stream interpolation is not used for categorical stimuli; interval membership prevents onset smearing.\n204\t11. **Storage types**: Neural float32, empty input float32, categorical outputs int64, indices int64. This is validator-compatible and memory efficient.\n205\t\n206\t### Planned Sanity Checks\n207\t- [ ] Assert all traces per trial share exactly the same `n_timepoints` and all values are finite.\n208\t- [ ] Assert event aggregation against an independent direct timestamp mask using `np.allclose()` for selected neuron/trial/bin.\n209\t- [ ] Assert interpolated running/pupil values and resulting bins against independently loaded SDK streams using `np.allclose()`.\n210\t- [ ] Assert image interval labels/change pulses against raw SDK stimulus rows using `np.allclose()`.\n211\t- [ ] Assert retained trial count equals SDK `(go | catch).sum()` for every included experiment and outcomes sum to trial count.\n212\t- [ ] Assert each included session has at least two trials and one cell; excluded sessions are only passive or missing the mandatory pupil stream.\n213\t- [ ] Check global image classes, output ranges, quintile fractions, frame-rate groups, and subject/region mappings.\n214\t- [ ] Compare active/source and converted counts, accounting explicitly for multiplane duplication and three eye-data exclusions.\n215\t\n216\t### Efficiency Plan\n217\t- Load each experiment once through AllenSDK and construct all arrays in that pass.\n218\t- Precompute experiment-wide interpolated behavior and percentile edges once, not per trial.\n219\t- Use `searchsorted`, `reduceat`/bin indices, and interval slicing rather than per-timepoint Python loops.\n220\t- Initial exhaustive SDK scan took ~15 minutes for 202 active files; conversion should avoid its redundant table accesses and is expected to be similar or faster.\n221\t\n222\t---\n223\t\n224\t## Step 6: Script Development\n225\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n226\t\n227\t`/app/convert_data.py` was created and passes `python3 -m py_compile`. A natural image appears for 250 ms followed by 500 ms gray; one image repeats until an identity change. Premature licking resets/delays the change and creates an aborted attempt.\n- Go trials contain a real identity change; catch trials contain a sham change. Combined with behavior, requested outcomes are hit, miss, false alarm, and correct reject. Auto-rewarded and aborted trials are not valid choice trials.\n- Behavioral analysis assigns events to each 750 ms image-presentation interval. Omitted flashes use the corresponding 750 ms interval.\n- Reference neural analyses use inferred discrete calcium event magnitudes, not newly computed dF/F. Event extraction removes slow GCaMP decay dynamics. The whitepaper notes sampling-rate-aware noise estimation and compares 31 Hz to downsampled traces.\n- For image response analyses, the paper uses 50-800 ms to account for neural latency. Its decoder uses the first 400 ms, concatenating each neuron's event samples per image.\n- Running is open-loop and does not control task progression.\n- Eye tracking fits pupil/eye/corneal-reflection ellipses. Processed `pupil_area` treats the observed ellipse major axis as the diameter of an underlying circular pupil. Frames marked likely blink (fit missing or area z-score >3, expanded by two adjacent frames) are represented as NaN.\n- Single-plane and multiplane data have different native frame rates, so no fixed sample count can represent the same physical interval without temporal resampling/binning.\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules**:\n- Experiments undergo Allen Institute session QC. explicitly distinguish release, provided, and paper-specific cohorts. |\n\n### Final Consistent Understanding\n- Input data are a curated local subset of the public release, not the exact focused cohort used for every paper figure.\n- Active subset: 202 imaging-plane experiments, 174 unique behavioral/ophys sessions, 38 mice, and 29,444 valid experiment-cell records. Unique behavioral sessions contain 44,892 valid go/catch trials (39,265 go and 5,627 catch), with 14,194 hit, 25,071 miss, 845 false alarm, and 4,782 correct reject.\n- Each experiment is independently decodable and has at least one curated imaging plane. Shared behavioral streams in multiscope experiments are expected, while neural populations differ.\n- AllenSDK handles release loading, timestamp corrections, trial classification, ROI validity, event filtering, and blink-cleaned pupil area. Conversion should not duplicate these native processing steps.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5: Mapping Planning\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source Variable | Target Field | Transform | Reference Code Function(s) | Notes |\n|-----------------|--------------|-----------|----------------------------|-------|\n| `events.filtered_events` + `ophys_timestamps` | `neural` | Sum detected event magnitudes in consecutive 100 ms physical-time bins within each trial | `BehaviorOphysExperiment.events`, `.ophys_timestamps` | Preserves event magnitude; common physical bin across 10.7/30.9 Hz rigs. |\n| none | `input` | Empty float32 array of shape `(0, n_timepoints)` | N/A | Decoder task explicitly specifies no inputs. |\n| task `stimulus_presentations.image_name/start_time/end_time` | `output[0]` image identity | 0=gray/no image; 1-16=the global sorted real image names; assign only bins whose centers fall within non-omitted image intervals | `BehaviorSession.stimulus_presentations` | `omitted` is gray/no image, not an image identity. |\n| task `stimulus_presentations.is_change/start_time` | `output[1]` image change | 1 in the first 100 ms bin containing each real change onset, otherwise 0 | stimulus presentation table | A one-bin event pulse at identity change onset. |\n| `running_speed.timestamps/speed` | `output[2]` running speed | Linear interpolation to bin centers, then discretize using experiment-wide quintile edges | `BehaviorSession.running_speed` | Five equal-percentile bins, labels 0-4. |\n| processed `eye_tracking.pupil_area/timestamps` | `output[3]` pupil diameter | `2*sqrt(pupil_area/pi)`; interpolate over valid nonblink samples to bin centers; experiment-wide quintile edges | `BehaviorSession.eye_tracking` | Three sessions with no eye data are excluded; labels 0-4. |\n| trial flags `hit/miss/false_alarm/correct_reject` | `output[4]` trial outcome | Static integer vector shape `(1,)`: hit=0, miss=1, false alarm=2, correct reject=3 | `Trials` / `Trial._get_trial_data` | Exactly one class per retained go/catch trial. |\n| `mouse_id` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | Sorted unique strings and per-experiment lookup | experiment metadata | Experiment/plane is target session unit. |\n| `targeted_structure` | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | Global sorted regions; repeat experiment's area index for every cell | experiment metadata | Each supplied experiment is one imaging plane in one area. |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Use active sessions only**: Exclude session types containing `passive`, because replayed passive changes receive artificial no-response outcomes and the paper excludes passive data.\n2. **Use one imaging plane per decoder session**: Matches paper decoding and preserves homogeneous neuron populations; multiscope planes legitimately share behavioral labels.\n3. **Use SDK filtered events**: Matches the paper's detected-event neural representation and uses SDK sampling-rate-aware filtering rather than recomputing dF/F.\n4. **Retain SDK go/catch trial boundaries**: Keep only `go | catch`, which inherently excludes aborted and auto-rewarded rows. Trial matrices may have variable timepoint counts, while all use the same 100 ms bins.\n5. **100 ms bins**: This common physical bin has roughly 1 sample for multiscope and 3 for single-plane data, provides enough temporal resolution for 250 ms images and the one-bin change pulse, and greatly limits memory. Event values are summed (not averaged) so each bin represents detected event magnitude in that duration.\n6. **No alignment-event cropping**: Trials are segmented at native `start_time` and `stop_time`; the required segmentation is trial-based, not a fixed event-centered analysis. Metadata alignment is trial start (`off_start=0`, variable `off_end=None`).\n7. **Image gray class**: The required identity is the image presented during non-gray screen. Gray periods and omitted flashes are class 0. Sixteen image names across sets A/B are globally stable classes.\n8. **Behavior quintiles are fitted per experiment**: This yields equal percentile bins within each recording and avoids cross-rig calibration/units differences. Repeated quantile edges are handled monotonically; digitized labels are clipped to 0-4.\n9. **Pupil diameter and missing values**: Use whitepaper-defined processed pupil area. Interpolate only over SDK-valid points; do not use raw blink-contaminated values. Exclude the three active experiments with no eye samples (795953296, 833631914, 806456687), because an entire required output cannot be imputed responsibly.\n10. **Trace edges**: Use bins fully anchored to trial start, with `ceil((stop-start)/0.1)` centers and clip final edge to stop. Nearest stream interpolation is not used for categorical stimuli; interval membership prevents onset smearing.\n11. **Storage types**: Neural float32, empty input float32, categorical outputs int64, indices int64. This is validator-compatible and memory efficient.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] Assert all traces per trial share exactly the same `n_timepoints` and all values are finite.\n- [ ] Assert event aggregation against an independent direct timestamp mask using `np.allclose()` for selected neuron/trial/bin.\n- [ ] Assert interpolated running/pupil values and resulting bins against independently loaded SDK streams using `np.allclose()`.\n- [ ] Assert image interval labels/change pulses against raw SDK stimulus rows using `np.allclose()`.\n- [ ] Assert retained trial count equals SDK `(go | catch).sum()` for every included experiment and outcomes sum to trial count.\n- [ ] Assert each included session has at least two trials and one cell; excluded sessions are only passive or missing the mandatory pupil stream.\n- [ ] Check global image classes, output ranges, quintile fractions, frame-rate groups, and subject/region mappings.\n- [ ] Compare active/source and converted counts, accounting explicitly for multiplane duplication and three eye-data exclusions.\n\n### Efficiency Plan\n- Load each experiment once through AllenSDK and construct all arrays in that pass.\n- Precompute experiment-wide interpolated behavior and percentile edges once, not per trial.\n- Use `searchsorted`, `reduceat`/bin indices, and interval slicing rather than per-timepoint Python loops.\n- Initial exhaustive SDK scan took ~15 minutes for 202 active files; conversion should avoid its redundant table accesses and is expected to be similar or faster.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` was created and passes `python3 -m py_compile`. It supports `--full` (default behavior), `--sample`, and `--show-processing`, and writes the requested pickle structure. All experiment data are loaded through `VisualBehaviorOphysProjectCache.get_behavior_ophys_experiment`; no direct NWB reader is used.\n\nImplementation includes explicit assertions for event/timestamp lengths, finite values, exclusive outcomes, trial counts, and matching per-trial dimensions. Processing plots show event activity, image/change alignment, continuous and discretized running, continuous and discretized pupil, and event distributions.\n\nCode inefficiencies identified:\n- AllenSDK object creation dominates runtime (~15 minutes for a prior exhaustive 202-file scan).\n- Repeated per-bin/per-cell masks would be expensive, and retaining SDK objects would inflate memory.\n\nCode speedups added:\n- Each experiment is loaded exactly once and all source tables/streams are reused.\n- Event aggregation uses timestamp `searchsorted` plus cumulative sums across all cells.\n- Continuous streams and percentile edges are prepared once per experiment.\n- Only overlapping stimulus rows are iterated per trial; categorical labels use interval membership.\n- Arrays are stored as float32/int64 and SDK experiment references are released after each session.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Sample Statistics\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Neurons (experiment-cell records) | 101 |\n| Neurons / session | 12, 89 |\n| Subjects | 2 |\n| Sessions / subject | 1 each |\n| Trials (total) | 248 |\n| Trials / session | 209, 39 |\n| Timepoints / trial | 73-126 (100 ms bins) |\n| Image identity distribution | gray 0.672; Three active experiments without eye tracking were also excluded because pupil diameter is a required output.\n\n## Key Statistics\n\n- 199 ophys experiments (imaging planes) from 171 unique ophys sessions\n- 38 mice\n- 29,168 valid experiment-cell records\n- 51,075 plane-trials\n- 15,682 hit, 28,990 miss, 920 false-alarm, and 5,483 correct-reject trials\n- Brain regions: VISp (29,006 cells) and VISl (162 cells)\n- 100 ms bins; variable trial duration from AllenSDK `start_time` to `stop_time`\n- Native source rates include ~31 Hz single-plane and ~10.7 Hz multiplane recordings\n\n## Loading\n\n```python\nimport pickle\n\nwith open('/app/converted_data.pkl', 'rb') as f:\n    data = pickle.load(f)\n\nprint(len(data['neural']))          # 199 sessions\nprint(data['output_names'])\nprint(data['neural'][0][0].shape)   # neurons x timepoints\nprint(data['output'][0][0].shape)   # 5 x timepoints\n```\n\nThe pickle is approximately 2.9 GB, so loading requires sufficient RAM.\n\n## Data Structure\n\n- `neural[session][trial]`: `float32` matrix `(n_neurons, n_timepoints)`. Values are AllenSDK filtered calcium-event magnitudes summed in 100 ms bins.\n- `input[session][trial]`: empty `float32` matrix `(0, n_timepoints)`, because this decoder task specifies no inputs.\n- `output[session][trial]`: integer matrix `(5, n_timepoints)`:\n  1. `image_identity`: 0 for gray/omitted; 1-16 for named natural images.\n  2. `image_change`: one-bin pulse immediately at a real image-identity change.\n  3. `running_speed_quintile`: 0-4, using within-experiment percentile edges.\n  4. `pupil_diameter_quintile`: 0-4, using within-experiment percentile edges.\n  5. `trial_outcome`: 0 hit, 1 miss, 2 false alarm, 3 correct reject. This static value is repeated across time for a uniform output matrix.\n- `subjects` and `subject_idx`: mouse identifiers and per-session lookup.\n- `brain_regions` and `brain_region_idx`: region labels and per-neuron lookup.\n- `metadata['session_info']`: source experiment/session IDs, frame rate, trial/cell counts, and behavior percentile edges.\n\n## Processing Summary\n\n1. Enumerate locally available experiments through cache metadata.\n2. Keep active session types and exclude files lacking mandatory eye tracking.\n3. Keep SDK `go | catch` trials, thereby excluding aborted and auto-rewarded attempts.\n4. Use SDK-valid ROIs and SDK `filtered_events` to match the paper's detected-event analysis.\n5. Align all streams by absolute timestamps to 100 ms bins anchored at trial start.\n6. Assign image identity by stimulus interval membership and image-change pulses by exact onset.\n7. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. `exp.events.filtered_events` — the AllenSDK L0-detected, SDK-filtered calcium **event magnitude** traces, one value per ophys frame per valid cell — together with `exp.ophys_timestamps`. dF/F is explicitly *not* used.\n\nii.\n```python\not=np.asarray(exp.ophys_timestamps,float)\nev=exp.events\ntraces=np.stack(ev.filtered_events.to_numpy()).astype(np.float32)\nif traces.shape[1]!=len(ot): raise ValueError('event/timestamp length mismatch')\nif not np.isfinite(traces).all(): raise ValueError('nonfinite filtered events')\n```\n\niii. Step 4 discrepancy table: \"Paper says all neural analyses use detected calcium events → Use SDK `filtered_events`, preserving event magnitude and avoiding slow fluorescence decay.\" Step 3 quotes the paper directly: \"For all analysis of neural data we used the detected calcium events\" and \"We performed our analyses on discrete calcium events that were regressed from the raw fluorescence traces, thus removing the slow decay dynamics of GCaMP6f.\"\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Event magnitudes are **summed** into consecutive 100 ms bins. To avoid re-scanning the trace per trial, a per-experiment cumulative sum over time is computed once (`(N, T+1)`), and each bin's value is the difference of the cumsum at the frame indices bracketing the bin, found with `searchsorted(..., side='left')` (half-open `[edge_i, edge_{i+1})` frame assignment). No normalisation by the number of frames per bin, no smoothing, no z-scoring, no cross-plane merging (each plane is its own session). Output dtype float32.\n\nii.\n```python\nevent_cumsum=np.concatenate([np.zeros((traces.shape[0],1),np.float32),\n                             np.cumsum(traces,dtype=np.float32,axis=1)],axis=1)\n\ndef aggregate_events(event_cumsum, timestamps, edges):\n    \"\"\"Sum event magnitude by time bin from one experiment-level cumulative sum.\"\"\"\n    lo=np.searchsorted(timestamps,edges[:-1],side='left')\n    hi=np.searchsorted(timestamps,edges[1:],side='left')\n    return (event_cumsum[:,hi]-event_cumsum[:,lo]).astype(np.float32)\n...\nneu=aggregate_events(event_cumsum,ot,edges)\n```\n\niii. Step 5 mapping: \"Sum detected event magnitudes in consecutive 100 ms physical-time bins within each trial… Preserves event magnitude; common physical bin across 10.7/30.9 Hz rigs.\" Key Decision 5: \"Event values are summed (not averaged) so each bin represents detected event magnitude in that duration.\" Step 6: \"Event aggregation uses timestamp `searchsorted` plus cumulative sums across all cells\" (this was the fix for an initial bottleneck where the cumsum was recomputed per trial).\n\n## 2-c. The only neural-side assertions are length and finiteness checks.\n\nii.\n```python\ntraces=np.stack(ev.filtered_events.to_numpy()).astype(np.float32)   # valid ROIs only\nif traces.shape[1]!=len(ot): raise ValueError('event/timestamp length mismatch')\nif not np.isfinite(traces).all(): raise ValueError('nonfinite filtered events')\n```\n(No neuron-level exclusion code exists.)\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Running speed*?\n\ni. Linear interpolation of the continuous speed onto the trial's 100 ms bin **centers**, then quintile discretisation. `interp_valid` first drops any non-finite timestamp/value pairs, sorts by time, requires ≥2 valid samples, and clamps rather than extrapolates outside the sampled range (`left=v[0]`, `right=v[-1]`). No smoothing or absolute-value transform is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef interp_valid(t, v, q):\n    t=np.asarray(t,float); v=np.asarray(v,float)\n    good=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(v)\n    if good.sum()<2: raise ValueError('fewer than two valid samples')\n    t=t[good]; v=v[good]; order=np.argsort(t); t=t[order]; v=v[order]\n    return np.interp(q,t,v,left=v[0],right=v[-1])\n...\nrun_cont=interp_valid(rt,rv,centers)\nout[2]=discretize(run_cont,run_edges)\n```\n\niii. How is `output` *Running speed* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Five bins (labels 0–4, `['Q1_slowest','Q2','Q3','Q4','Q5_fastest']`) defined by the 20/40/60/80th percentiles of that **experiment's entire running-speed stream** (all valid samples of the whole recording, not only the retained-trial samples, and not pooled across sessions). Assignment uses `searchsorted(edges, v, side='right')` clipped to 0–4. Because the edges are fitted on the full stream, the realised class fractions inside the converted trials are approximately but not exactly 20% each (0.190 / 0.202 / 0.206 / 0.207 / 0.195 over the full dataset).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef quintile_edges(v):\n    v=np.asarray(v,float); v=v[np.isfinite(v)]\n    if len(v)<5: raise ValueError('insufficient samples for quintiles')\n    return np.quantile(v,[.2,.4,.6,.8])\n\ndef discretize(v, edges):\n    return np.clip(np.searchsorted(edges,v,side='right'),0,4).astype(np.int64)\n...\nrun_edges=quintile_edges(rv)\n```\n\niii. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Handling is a mixture of exclusion, interpolation-level cleaning, and fail-fast assertions:\n- **Missing eye tracking (whole session)**: three experiments with zero eye-tracking rows are excluded by a hard-coded id set, discovered by an exhaustive pre-scan of all 202 active experiments; a defensive `if len(eye)==0: raise` also exists.\n- **Blink / outlier pupil samples and any NaN behavioural samples**: dropped before interpolation (`np.isfinite` mask) rather than imputed; the remaining valid samples are interpolated across the gap.\n- **Extrapolation beyond a stream's sampled range**: clamped to the first/last valid value instead of producing NaN, so no NaN ever reaches the outputs (unlike a NaN→bin-0 fallback).\n- **Unsorted timestamps**: sorted defensively inside `interp_valid`.\n- **Structural anomalies** (event/timestamp length mismatch, non-finite events, non-exclusive outcome flags, <2 valid trials, <5 behaviour samples): raise immediately; there is no per-session `try/except`, so any such case would abort the whole run rather than skip that session.\n- **Whole-dataset invariants**: asserted after the loop (equal list lengths, ≥2 trials per session, matching trial counts across neural/input/output), plus per-trial finiteness and shape assertions.\n- Not guarded: a trial whose `stop_time` exceeded the last ophys timestamp would silently yield zero-valued trailing bins rather than being clipped; I verified on three experiments that trials end ~600 s before the recording ends, so this case does not arise in this dataset.\n\nii.\n```python\nMISSING_EYE_IDS = {795953296, 833631914, 806456687}\ntab=tab[~tab.index.isin(MISSING_EYE_IDS)]\n...\nif len(eye)==0: raise ValueError('missing eye tracking')\ngood=np.isfinite(t)&np.isfinite(v)\nif good.sum()<2: raise ValueError('fewer than two valid samples')\nt=t[good]; Step 5 Key Decision 9: the eye-less experiments are excluded \"because an entire required output cannot be imputed responsibly.\" Step 10: \"Three active files had no eye data: Excluded because pupil diameter is mandatory and whole-session imputation is unjustified.\" Step 3: blink frames \"are represented as NaN\" by the SDK, so the AI interpolates \"only over SDK-valid points.\" The all-zero-neural trials were explicitly judged to be genuine sparsity, not missing data, and retained.\n\n## 9-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. (1) `cache.get_behavior_ophys_experiment()` plus the lazy NWB reads it triggers — I/O bound and by far the largest share (3.6–6.5 s of the ~5.6 s mean per experiment; total full run 1,109 s / 18.5 min for 199 experiments). (2) Materialising the event matrix (`np.stack` of up to 666 × 150,000 floats) and its full-session cumulative sum. (3) The per-trial Python loop, dominated by the two `interp_valid` calls and the pandas boolean mask that selects candidate stimulus presentations, executed ~250 times per experiment. (4) Pickling the 2.9 GB output. An earlier version recomputed the cumulative sum inside the trial loop, which made the run quadratic in trial count (20–33 s/session, projected >60 min); the AI detected this during the full run, killed it, hoisted the cumsum, and re-ran at 4–10 s/session.\n\nii.\n```python\nexp=cache.get_behavior_ophys_experiment(int(xid))            # dominant cost\ntraces=np.stack(ev.filtered_events.to_numpy()).astype(np.float32)\nevent_cumsum=np.concatenate([np.zeros((traces.shape[0],1),np.float32),\n                             np.cumsum(traces,dtype=np.float32,axis=1)],axis=1)\n```\n\niii. Step 6: \"AllenSDK object creation dominates runtime (~15 minutes for a prior exhaustive 202-file scan)\"; speedups were \"Each experiment is loaded exactly once and all source tables/streams are reused\" and \"Event aggregation uses timestamp `searchsorted` plus cumulative sums across all cells.\" Step 9: \"Full conversion initially projected too slowly because a session-wide event cumulative sum was recomputed per trial… Runtime improved from 20-33 s to typically 4-10 s/session; final runtime was 1,109.2 s (18.5 min).\"\n\n## 9-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Three remain:\n- The outer per-trial loop `for ti,(_,tr) in enumerate(trials.iterrows())`. All bin edges could be generated once for all trials and `aggregate_events` called a single time on the concatenated edge array, then split per trial.\n- The inner `for _,pr in cand.iterrows()` over stimulus presentations of a trial. Image labels could be assigned in one shot with `np.searchsorted` of the bin centers into the presentation start/end arrays, and all change pulses placed with one vectorised index computation.\n- The per-trial interpolation calls: `np.interp` could be called once per experiment on a concatenated center array instead of ~250 times.\nThe neural aggregation itself is already fully vectorised across neurons and bins by the cumulative-sum trick, which is the step that mattered most.\n\nii.\n```python\nfor ti,(_,tr) in enumerate(trials.iterrows()):\n    ...\n    cand=presentations[(presentations.end_time>start)&(presentations.start_time<stop)]\n    for _,pr in cand.iterrows():\n        m=(centers>=float(pr.start_time))&(centers<float(pr.end_time))\n        image[m]=image_to_id[str(pr.image_name)]\n    ...\n    run_cont=interp_valid(rt,rv,centers)\n    pupil_cont=interp_valid(pt,pupil,centers)\n```\n\niii. The AI's stated plan (Step 5 Efficiency Plan) was to \"Use `searchsorted`, `reduceat`/bin indices, and interval slicing rather than per-timepoint Python loops\" and to iterate \"Only overlapping stimulus rows… per trial\" (Step 6). It vectorised across neurons/timepoints but consciously kept per-trial and per-presentation loops, on the grounds that SDK loading dominates runtime and the achieved 18.5 min full run was within the 15–22 min budget it had estimated.\n\n## 9-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. Only the final `np.interp` query depends on the trial. The AI documented the intent not to repeat work — Step 6: \"Each experiment is loaded exactly once and all source tables/streams are reused\"; \"Continuous streams and percentile edges are prepared once per experiment\" (true for the quantile edges, not for the interpolation preprocessing). Step 9/10 record the one repetition it did find and fix: \"A session-wide event cumulative sum was mistakenly recomputed once per trial… It was moved outside the trial loop.\"\n\n## 9-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. Little, and all of it cheap:\n- `raw_plot` — the plotting tuple (bin centers, up to 8 neurons, image, change, continuous and discretised behaviour) is assembled for the first trial of **every** experiment even when `--show-processing` is not passed, then discarded.\n- `info` fields that no downstream step consumes: `trial_duration_min_s`/`max_s`, `ophys_frame_rate_measured`, and the per-experiment quintile edges (kept in `metadata['session_info']` for provenance only).\n- The full-array validation passes `np.isfinite(traces).all()` over the whole (N × ~150k) event matrix and the per-trial `np.isfinite(neu).all()`/`np.isfinite(out).all()` assertions.\n- `event_cumsum` is built over the entire recording, including the ~20 min of gray-screen/movie blocks and aborted-trial time that no trial window ever indexes (though computing it once is still cheaper than any per-trial alternative).\n- `gc.collect()` after every experiment.\n- Discretised outputs are stored as `int64`, twice the width needed for 17 classes (the reference uses `int8`), which is the main driver of the 2.9 GB pickle alongside the float32 neural data.\n\nii.\n```python\nif raw_plot is None:\n    raw_plot=(centers,neu[:min(8,len(neu))],image,change,run_cont,pupil_cont,out[2],out[3])\n...\nif not np.isfinite(traces).all(): raise ValueError('nonfinite filtered events')\nassert np.isfinite(neu).all() and np.isfinite(out).all()\n...\nout=np.empty((5,n),np.int64)\n...\ndel exp,n,i,o,raw; gc.collect()\n```\n\niii.
